rounds.text: Global Health Ltd commands an impressive rules-based screen score of 85 out of 100 with a medium confidence BUY rating, driven by robust top-line momentum with sales growing at 26% over the trailing twelve months and 34% YoY [E17, E58, E59]. Profitability quality remains exceptionally high, backed by a stellar 5-year profit growth CAGR of 80.7% and a strong cash conversion ratio of 1.29x where reported profits are fully backed by actual operating cash flows of Rs 714 Cr in March 2026 [E19, E31, E32, E56]. Furthermore, the business consistently outperforms sector benchmarks across core efficiency metrics, delivering an ROCE of 16.02% to 17.4% and an ROE of 14.3% to 15.2% against sector medians of 11.59% and 10.32% respectively [E8, E9, E10, E12, E13]. Institutional backing is strengthening as domestic institutions expanded their stake significantly to 17.01% alongside positive institutional money flow, all supported by a powerful healthcare sector tailwind score of +0.78 [E40, E41, E67]. Technical strength mirrors this fundamental excellence, with the stock trading above both its 50-day and 200-day moving averages in a golden cross setup, accompanied by a solid Sharpe ratio of 1.08 [E47, E52]. Conceded: the stock trades at an elevated valuation including a P/E of 59.8 to 62.66x and a price-to-book ratio of 8.94x, alongside a discounted cash flow intrinsic value estimate of Rs 929 that reflects considerable market expectations already priced in [E1, E2, E6, E42, E64].

Global Health Ltd (Medanta) trades at extreme valuation multiples that are entirely disconnected from conservative intrinsic value models, with a price-to-earnings ratio of 59.8x [E1] and a price-to-book ratio of 8.94x [E2], both towering far above sector benchmarks of 30.53x and 2.92x respectively [E6, E7]. This aggressive pricing is further underscored by a negligible dividend yield of 0.03% [E4] and a discounted cash flow valuation pointing to an intrinsic value of just Rs 929 per share against a market price of Rs 1,440, resulting in an alarming margin of safety of -55.0% [E42, E43]. Furthermore, a reverse DCF reveals that the current market price aggressively prices in 24.1% earnings growth, which significantly outstrips the 18.0% growth assumed in the base case [E44]. Fundamental execution also displays underlying pressures, as evidenced by a negative free cash flow of Rs -123 Cr in March 2026 [E33], rising borrowings of Rs 1,353 Cr [E36], and a three-year operating margin contraction of 3 percentage points down to 22% [E27]. Conceded: [E19].

Conceded: [E1] and [E2]. However, the premium valuation is fully justified by elite operational returns that dwarf sector benchmarks, including an ROCE of 16.02% against a sector 11.59% and an ROE of 14.3% versus 10.32% [E10, E9]. The bear's reliance on static DCF models ignores accelerating top-line momentum, evidenced by a 26% TTM sales growth rate and 25% compounded sales growth over five years [E17, E15]. Furthermore, operating margin contraction is a stale trailing indicator, contradicted by recent quarterly performance showing a 4 percentage point expansion to 25% and a consistent four-quarter upward trend [E28, E30]. While free cash flow dipped, operating cash flow reached a robust Rs 714 Cr with a 1.29x cash conversion, proving that reported profits are fully backed by hard cash [E32, E31]. Finally, institutional confidence is surging rather than fleeing, demonstrated by domestic institutions increasing their stake by 5.86 percentage points and driving a positive money flow signal [E40, E41].

Conceded: [E10] and [E9]. However, the bull's dismissal of valuation ignores that the stock trades at an exorbitant P/E of 59.8x and a price-to-book ratio of 8.94x, which severely outstrips sector benchmarks of 30.53x and 2.92x [E1, E2, E6, E7]. The reliance on trailing sales momentum is offset by the reality that operating margins over the trailing twelve months have actually contracted by 3 percentage points to 22% compared to three years prior [E27]. Furthermore, while operating cash flow reached Rs 714 Cr, free cash flow collapsed to Rs -123 Cr [E32, E33], exposing capital drains not captured by profit-to-cash conversions. The argument regarding institutional confidence is also selective, omitting that foreign institutions have reduced their holding by 1.44 percentage points [E39]. Finally, the current market price aggressively prices in 24.1% earnings growth—vastly exceeding the 18.0% base case—leaving the stock vulnerable to a -55% margin of safety deficit [E42, E43, E44].
